title: Learning Factors in AI-Augmented Education: A Comparative Study of Middle and High School Students
extended_summary:
This paper examines how four learning-related perception factors—experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation—relate to one another in AI-mediated educational settings, and whether these relationships differ between younger and older secondary students. The authors argue that prior work on AI in education has focused largely on higher education and often treats student perceptions as isolated outcomes rather than as interconnected dimensions that may vary by developmental stage.

The study investigated students’ perceptions after participating in AI-supported programming activities in extracurricular computer science courses. It used a 17-item instrument combining Likert-scale survey questions with open-ended responses, and analyzed the data through quantitative correlation analysis, group comparisons using Mann-Whitney U tests, and text-mining of written reflections. The AI tools differed by group: middle school students used Teachable Machine and chatbot interactions in an introductory AI course, while high school students used large language models such as Gemini and Claude for Python development and prompting-related activities.

Participants were 53 students in total from the University of Bologna’s extracurricular school context in Italy: 25 middle school students aged 10–13 and 28 high school students aged 15–20. The activities took place in authentic instructional settings connected to programming courses, with AI introduced as a final module. Data collection focused on students’ self-reported perceptions of usability, clarity, comfort, motivation, and overall experience.

The main conclusion is that developmental stage appears to moderate how students evaluate AI-supported learning. Middle school students showed strong positive correlations across all four dimensions, suggesting a holistic evaluation style in which positive impressions in one area generalized to others. High school students showed weaker and more differentiated relationships among dimensions, indicating a more independent and critical assessment of clarity, comfort, and motivation. The authors conclude that AI integration strategies in education should be tailored by age, with more structured and clarity-focused support for younger learners and more technically sophisticated, autonomy-supportive approaches for older students.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's generative AI assistant/LLM family used for conversational prompting and content generation.
identified_tools.use_case: High school students used Gemini during programming learning activities to develop Python applications with vibe coding and prompting.

findings.finding_summary: In the high school group using LLMs such as Gemini and Claude for Python application development, students reported generally positive perceptions of AI-supported learning. High school students reported higher ease of use than middle school students on Q3 (M=3.68 vs. 3.16; U=192.00, p=0.0013), and their perceptions were more differentiated across dimensions rather than globally coupled.
findings.measure: Questionnaire perceptions of ease of use and learning dimensions (experience, clarity, comfort, motivation) in AI-supported programming activities

findings.finding_summary: For high school students using LLMs such as Gemini and Claude, dimension-level correlations showed moderate coupling between Experience and Clarity (rho=0.51) but weak or near-zero relationships between Experience and Motivation (rho=0.02) and Experience and Comfort (rho=0.16). This indicates students saw the tool as useful and clear without necessarily finding it motivating or comfortable.
findings.measure: Spearman correlations among aggregated perception dimensions

identified_tools.name: Teachable Machine
identified_tools.description: Google's web-based tool for building simple machine learning classification models through hands-on examples.
identified_tools.use_case: Middle school students used Teachable Machine for introductory AI activities including hands-on classification and chatbot interaction within a broader computer science curriculum.

findings.finding_summary: Middle school students using Teachable Machine in introductory AI activities showed generally positive perceptions, but lower ease of use than the high school LLM group. On Q3, middle school students reported M=3.16 versus 3.68 for high school students, with a statistically significant group difference (U=192.00, p=0.0013).
findings.measure: Questionnaire perceptions of ease of use and learning dimensions in AI-supported learning

findings.finding_summary: For middle school students, all aggregated learning dimensions were positively and substantially correlated, indicating a holistic evaluation pattern of the AI tool. Reported correlations included Experience–Clarity rho=0.79, Clarity–Motivation rho=0.60, Q1–Q6 rho=0.74, and Q8–Q14 rho=0.72.
findings.measure: Spearman correlations among questionnaire items and aggregated perception dimensions

quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary mixed-methods cross-sectional study using surveys, correlations, Mann-Whitney tests, and text mining in authentic classrooms, but it is not an experimental or quasi-experimental design and reports perception outcomes rather than direct achievement effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports generally positive and mixed perception differences with some statistically significant group differences, but no standardized learning effect sizes or direct academic outcome impacts are reported, making overall impact unclear.
